history.vet: The vet found nothing left to fix and raised two calls for you.

declinedFindings.summary: Add a calorie count to every recipe on the plan.
declinedFindings.reason: Nothing in your framing asks for nutrition numbers, so adding them would be new scope.

declinedFindings.summary: Let two people edit the same plan at once.
declinedFindings.reason: You said the planner is for one household cook, so sharing a plan is out of scope.

cards.question: Should leftovers from one dinner count as lunch the next day?

blocks.paragraph: The spec fills seven dinners and seven lunches, but it never says whether last night's dinner can be tomorrow's lunch. This one is yours to call, because it depends on whether households want to plan around leftovers or cook fresh every time.

bullets: If leftovers count, plans need fewer recipes and shopping lists get shorter.
If they do not, every meal is a new recipe, so plans stay varied but take more cooking.

context.title: The line that leaves it open

blocks.quote: Each day has one breakfast, one lunch and one dinner slot, and every slot is filled with a different recipe.

options.label: Let leftovers fill a lunch slot
options.consequence: Plans need fewer recipes and shopping lists get shorter, but the same recipe can show up twice in a day.

options.label: Require a different recipe for every slot
options.consequence: Every meal is a new recipe, so plans stay varied but need more cooking and a longer shopping list.

recommendation.text: Let leftovers fill a lunch slot.
recommendation.reason: Most weekly planners are used to save effort, and leftover lunches are the common way to do that.

cards.question: Do you want past weekly plans kept after the week ends?

blocks.paragraph: The spec covers making and editing the current week's plan. It says nothing about what happens to that plan once the week is over. Keeping old plans means more storage and a new screen to browse them, so it is a call about scope.
